questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presented with a foul-smelling right lower extremity soft tissue infection. He was obese and had a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, anemia, hyperlipidemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and a recent deep vein thrombosis. He had no known drug allergies. Home medications were ferrous sulfate 325 mg PO TD, tizanidine 2 mg PO BD, theophylline 300 mg PO BD, warfarin 5 mg PO daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg PO daily. On examination, he was afebrile with an infected ulcer on his right lower leg. Investigations: Total white cell count 9800 cells/mm3 MRI: no evidence of underlying osteomyelitis Wound swab culture: mixed organisms including Pseudomonas isolated Plans were to treat the infection with ciprofloxacin PO and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid PO.
questions.lead_in: What medication would be most likely to interfere with the effectiveness of this planned antibiotic regimen?
questions.explanation: Ferrous sulfate Atorvastatin would not be expected to interact with the planned antibiotic regimen. Ciprofloxacin can significantly increase serum concentrations of theophylline, tizanidine, and warfarin and should be avoided in combination with these agents. Polyvalent metallic cations, such as ferrous sulfate, can adsorb oral fluoroquinolone doses and dramatically reduce systemic exposure and clinical effects of the fluoroquinolone.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q5

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man presented with fever, rigors, neck pain, and respiratory distress. He had had a sore throat for the preceding week. On examination, his heart rate was 148 beats/minute, temperature 38.5°C, blood pressure 82/54 mmHg, SaO2 89% on room air. Examination of the oropharynx showed erythema over the soft palate and swollen tonsils. His neck movements were restricted, and there was tenderness and induration over the right jugular vein. Investigations: Peripheral white cell count 28.7 ×109/L (4.0–11.0) Platelets 67 ×109/L (150–400) CXR: multifocal bilateral infiltrates CT neck:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Fusobacterium necrophorum Lemierre’s syndrome is characterized by thrombosis and suppurative thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein. It is associated with disseminated septic emboli to the lungs and other sites. The most common pathogen is Fusobacterium necrophorum, but other organisms implicated include Eikenella, Bacteroides, and streptococcal species. Organisms may be isolated from blood cultures and from infective metastases. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q48

questions.question: A 24-year-old male presents with fever, hypotension, and worsening respiratory distress. CT shows bilateral rounded opacities and a left-sided empyema. One week ago he had a sore throat, which has now worsened.
questions.question_raw: A 24yo old male presents with fever, hypotension, worsening respiratory distress. CT shows bilateral opacities (rounded) and a left sided empyema. A week ago, the patient had a sore throat. This has now worsened.

parts.text: List the syndrome and the organism.

parts_raw.text: List the syndrome and the organism.

questions.model_answer: Syndrome: Lemierre syndrome (jugular vein septic thrombophlebitis) with septic pulmonary emboli seeding the lungs (cavitary/rounded opacities) and empyema, arising from an antecedent oropharyngeal infection. Organism: Fusobacterium necrophorum.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort listed invasive GAS/toxic shock as a possibility, but the antecedent sore throat with septic pulmonary emboli and empyema is the classic Lemierre/F. necrophorum picture the text describes.

cohort_answer.text: ?Invasive GAS/toxic shock syndrome, Streptococcus pyogenes; ?Lemierre's syndrome from Fusobacterium.

questions.model_answer: a) Lemierre syndrome (septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with septic pulmonary emboli). b) Fusobacterium necrophorum. c) Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck; expected finding is internal jugular vein thrombosis/thrombophlebitis. d) CT of the chest to evaluate the septic pulmonary emboli and detect empyema (feared complication; emboli may cavitate or cause empyema). e) A beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor such as piperacillin-tazobactam (F. necrophorum is often penicillin resistant), providing anaerobic and aerobic coverage.

questions.model_answer: a) Lemierre syndrome (internal jugular vein septic thrombophlebitis with septic pulmonary emboli). b) Fusobacterium necrophorum. c) Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck; expected to show internal jugular vein thrombosis. d) Blood cultures (bacteremia is universally present) and CT chest for septic emboli/empyema. e) Piperacillin-tazobactam, or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, for 4-6 weeks; anticoagulation remains controversial with limited evidence.

parts.text: Name two typical organisms that would not be covered by amoxicillin therapy alone.
Name two organisms that would not be covered by metronidazole alone.
Why does metronidazole only work for anaerobes?

parts_raw.text: Name 2 typical organisms that would not be covered by amoxicillin therapy alone
Name 2 organisms that would not be covered by metronidazole alone
Why does metronidazole only work for anaerobes.

questions.model_answer: a) Beta-lactamase-producing oral anaerobic gram-negative bacteria, which account for penicillin/amoxicillin failure: (1) pigmented Prevotella spp. (2) Fusobacterium spp. (Porphyromonas spp. also acceptable). b) Metronidazole has no aerobic/facultative activity, so it misses: (1) viridans (and other) streptococci (2) Actinomyces spp. c) Metronidazole is a prodrug requiring reductive activation: only obligate anaerobes possess the low-redox-potential electron-transport proteins (pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase/ferredoxin) that reduce its nitro group to cytotoxic nitroso radicals, which then fragment bacterial DNA. Aerobes lack this reductive machinery (and oxygen re-oxidizes any activated drug), so the drug is never activated in them.
questions.beyond_mandell: Metronidazole's reductive-activation mechanism is not stated in this chapter; it is standard antimicrobial pharmacology (Mandell antibacterial-agents chapters).
